front: Why is testing generative AI different from testing traditional software?
back: Traditional software is judged by exact behavior (does the function return the right value?). Generative AI can produce many acceptable answers, and a fluent answer can still be unsafe, ungrounded, slow, brittle, or expensive - so AI evaluation stacks multiple layers of testing instead of one pass/fail assertion.

front: What is MedEval's role, and what does it deliberately NOT do?
back: MedEval is the framework layer: it gives data models, evaluators, runners, and analysis utilities. It does not generate model outputs itself, and does not ship a CLI or application adapters.

front: What do Sections 1-16 vs. Sections 17-20 of the AI Testing Handbook cover?
back: Sections 1-16 stay entirely inside the framework layer (in-memory objects, no DB/network/real LLM). Sections 17-20 introduce the separate 'medai' repository to show a real pluggable LLM client, a real database with setup/teardown, and CI pipelines wiring it together - the product layer.

front: What is a golden dataset?
back: A curated set of inputs plus trusted labels/expectations - e.g., the raw prompt/input, structured facts expected to appear, facts that must never be invented, and optionally reference summaries, relevant retrieved documents, and source text.

front: Where is the core ClinicalCase schema defined, and what fields does it have?
back: src/medeval/models.py. Fields: id, text, symptoms, medications, required_facts, forbidden_facts, gold_summary, plus optional relevant_doc_ids, source_text, is_adversarial, adversarial_type.

front: What fields does load_cases() in src/medeval/dataset.py fail to preserve?
back: relevant_doc_ids, source_text, is_adversarial, and adversarial_type. Build ClinicalCase objects directly if you need those fields.

front: Interview framing: what makes a good AI test case?
back: It's not just an input/output pair - it carries enough structure to support multiple evaluators from the same row.

front: What is an exact-match evaluator?
back: One that scores outputs using deterministic string or set comparisons - cheap, reproducible, and ideal for structured targets like medication lists or required sections.

front: Where is MedicationF1Evaluator implemented, and what does it return?
back: src/medeval/evaluators/medication_f1.py. Returns med_precision, med_recall, med_f1, computed from normalized set overlap between gold and predicted medications.

front: Example: gold meds = [aspirin, nitroglycerin], predicted = [aspirin, metoprolol]. What are med_precision/recall/f1?
back: All three equal 0.5 (1 true positive out of 2 predicted and out of 2 gold).

front: Interview framing: why use exact-match metrics as a first line of defense?
back: They are fast, stable, and easy to debug for structured fields.

front: What defines a deterministic evaluator?
back: It always gives the same result for the same input - it never drifts because a judge model changed its mind.

front: Name three deterministic evaluators in MedEval and their files.
back: RequiredFactsEvaluator (evaluators/required_facts.py), ForbiddenFactsEvaluator (evaluators/forbidden_facts.py), FormatValidator (evaluators/format_validator.py).

front: What does RequiredFactsEvaluator return?
back: required_facts_score (fraction of required facts present in the summary text) and required_missing (list of missing facts).

front: What does ForbiddenFactsEvaluator return?
back: forbidden_score (0.0 if any forbidden fact was found, else 1.0) and forbidden_found (the list of forbidden facts actually found).

front: What is the exact exported class name for MedEval's format-checking evaluator?
back: FormatValidator (NOT 'FormatValidatorEvaluator' - that name doesn't exist and was a dead-code bug found by pylint, see Section 20).

front: Interview framing: how should you describe deterministic evaluators?
back: As policy checks - often the most defensible metrics in regulated or high-risk domains.

front: What problem does semantic similarity solve that exact match can't?
back: Recognizing correct paraphrases - e.g., 'heart attack' and 'myocardial infarction' mean the same thing but look unrelated as raw strings.

front: Does MedEval ship real embeddings or a full semantic-similarity stack?
back: No. It ships a lightweight LLMJudge protocol plus a deterministic fallback (DeterministicJudge) in src/medeval/llm_judge.py.

front: How does DeterministicJudge score two texts?
back: 1.0 if identical after lowercasing; 0.8 if gold words are a subset of predicted words; otherwise 0.5 (also 0.5 if either text is empty).

front: Interview framing: why say plainly when a component is a 'stub' or heuristic?
back: Credibility comes from knowing the boundary between demo logic and production logic.

front: What is 'LLM-as-a-judge'?
back: Using one model to assess the output of another model - a practical way to score open-ended text where exact-match rules are too brittle.

front: What protocol must a custom judge implement to plug into LLMJudgeEvaluator?
back: The LLMJudge protocol: a single method judge(self, gold_text: str, pred_text: str) -> float.

front: Where does LLMJudgeEvaluator live, and what does it return?
back: src/medeval/evaluators/llm_judge.py. Returns {'llm_judge_score': score}.

front: Interview framing: why does MedEval use a protocol instead of hard-coding an LLM provider?
back: So teams can plug in GPT, Claude, local models, or deterministic mocks interchangeably.

front: Why is human evaluation considered the gold standard for nuanced tasks?
back: Humans can judge safety, usefulness, and subtle factuality in ways automated metrics often miss.

front: What fields does the HumanRating dataclass capture?
back: case_id, rater_id, accuracy, safety, helpfulness (1-5 scales), has_errors, error_types, free_text_feedback.

front: What does HumanEvaluationWorkflow.calculate_inter_rater_reliability do?
back: Computes agreement statistics such as simple agreement rate and Cohen's Kappa, when exactly two raters are present.

front: Interview framing: what makes human evaluation itself an engineering problem?
back: Rubric design, multiple raters, agreement measurement, and outlier-rater detection all matter.

front: In RAG systems, why evaluate retrieval separately from generation?
back: A bad final answer may be caused by bad retrieval, not bad generation - if the right documents never make it into context, the generator has little chance of producing a grounded answer.

front: Where is RetrievalEvaluator implemented, and what metrics does it return?
back: src/medeval/evaluators/retrieval.py. Returns retrieval_precision@k, retrieval_recall@k, retrieval_f1@k, retrieval_mrr, retrieval_ndcg@k, num_relevant_retrieved, num_retrieved, num_relevant_total.

front: What does MRR stand for in retrieval metrics?
back: Mean Reciprocal Rank.

front: What does NDCG stand for in retrieval metrics?
back: Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain.

front: Define precision in plain terms.
back: 'When the system said yes, how often was it right?' = relevant retrieved / total retrieved.

front: Define recall in plain terms.
back: 'Of all the things it should have found, how many did it find?' = relevant retrieved / total relevant.

front: What is F1 (the formula)?
back: The harmonic balance of precision and recall: 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall).

front: Example: you retrieved 5 docs, 2 are relevant, and 3 relevant docs exist in total. What are precision@5 and recall@5?
Interview framing: why might you accept lower precision for higher recall?
back: In safety-critical contexts, higher recall catches more dangerous misses, even at the cost of more false positives.

front: What is a hallucination, in the AI-testing sense?
back: Unsupported generated content: facts, medications, numbers, or claims that the source material never justified. In medicine this can be actively harmful.

front: Where is HallucinationDetectorEvaluator implemented, and what does it return?
back: src/medeval/evaluators/hallucination.py. Returns hallucination_detected, hallucination_score, hallucination_types, forbidden_facts_found, unsupported_medications, num_violations.

front: Interview framing: how do you distinguish 'wrong because incomplete' from hallucination?
back: Hallucination testing focuses specifically on fabrication and unsupported claims, not omissions.

front: How does faithfulness differ from hallucination detection?
back: Faithfulness is narrower: it asks 'is this supported by the supplied context?' rather than the broader 'is this true?'

front: Where is FaithfulnessEvaluator implemented, and what happens if case.source_text is missing?
back: src/medeval/evaluators/hallucination.py (same module as hallucination detection). It returns an empty result if there is no source_text.

front: What does FaithfulnessEvaluator return?
back: faithfulness_score, grounded_sentences, total_sentences, ungrounded_claims (top 3), num_ungrounded.

front: How does MedEval's faithfulness check actually work under the hood?
back: A simple heuristic: it splits the prediction into sentences and checks content-word overlap against case.source_text.

front: Interview framing: how would you upgrade MedEval's current faithfulness check?
back: It's currently heuristic (word overlap); you could upgrade it with NLI (natural language inference), embeddings, or a stronger judge model.

front: What's the difference between safety testing and adversarial testing?
back: Safety testing checks whether a model avoids dangerous/overconfident/policy-violating behavior. Adversarial testing deliberately probes failure modes instead of only happy paths.

front: Where is SafetyGuardEvaluator implemented, and what does it return?
back: src/medeval/evaluators/safety.py. Returns safety_passed, safety_score, safety_violations, num_violations, requires_human_review.

front: What kinds of dangerous patterns does SafetyGuardEvaluator look for?
back: Telling a patient to stop medication or ignore a doctor, overconfident claims, and missing disclaimers.

front: What is prompt injection?
back: A security attack where the user tries to override the model's intended instructions or extract hidden context.

front: What does PromptInjectionDetectorEvaluator check, and where does it live?
back: src/medeval/evaluators/safety.py. Checks both the input text (for injection patterns) and the output text (for leaked instructions).

front: What does PromptInjectionDetectorEvaluator return?
back: injection_detected, injection_score, injection_patterns, suspicious_phrases, output_leaked_instructions, model_rejected_attack, is_adversarial_input.

front: Interview framing: what's the difference between 'detecting an attack pattern' and 'model_rejected_attack'?
back: Detecting the pattern just means recognizing an attempt exists; model_rejected_attack measures whether the model safely resisted it - they are not the same metric.

front: What does robustness testing measure?
back: Whether a model behaves consistently when the input is noisy, misspelled, paraphrased, or otherwise slightly perturbed.

front: Where is AdversarialRobustnessEvaluator implemented, and how does it decide a case is a perturbation test?
back: src/medeval/evaluators/safety.py. It checks whether case.is_adversarial is True AND case.adversarial_type is one of 'perturbation', 'typos', or 'paraphrase'.

front: What does AdversarialRobustnessEvaluator return for a baseline (non-perturbed) case?
back: robustness_score, consistency_with_baseline, passed_robustness_test, and variation_type are all None; is_baseline is True.

front: Interview framing: what is robustness testing NOT asking for?
back: Perfection - it's asking that small input noise doesn't cause a catastrophic failure (graceful degradation).

front: Besides accuracy, what else matters for a production AI system?
back: Response time (latency), token usage, cost, availability, and timeout behavior.

front: Where is PerformanceEvaluator implemented, and what does it return?
back: src/medeval/evaluators/performance.py. Returns latency_ms, cost_usd, tokens_used, passed_latency_sla, passed_cost_sla.

front: What does ReliabilityEvaluator return?
back: prediction_succeeded, is_error, is_timeout, error_type, availability.

front: Interview framing: what tradeoff should you mention regarding picking 'the best model'?
back: Multi-objective optimization: the best model is often the one that hits the quality target while staying inside latency and cost budgets, not simply the highest-accuracy one at any cost.

front: What is regression testing in the AI-model context?
back: Asking whether a new model version got worse compared to a previous baseline.

front: What is a quality gate?
back: A rule that turns the regression question into a deploy/no-deploy decision.

front: How does EvaluationRunner's built-in quality_gate_passed differ from the standalone quality_gate.py/baseline.py modules?
back: The standalone modules perform explicit threshold checks. The runner's built-in flag is simpler: if baseline_path is set, it just checks whether every *_mean metric is at least quality_gate_threshold.

front: Interview framing: why should quality gates be metric-specific?
back: A harmless drop in one metric may be acceptable, but a safety regression usually is not - not all metric drops deserve equal blocking power.

front: What does statistical comparison determine?
back: Whether a difference between two models is likely real or just noise.

front: What does calibration measure?
back: Whether a model's stated confidence matches its actual accuracy in reality.

front: What fields are in the ComparisonResult dataclass?
back: metric_name, baseline_mean, candidate_mean, difference, percent_change, confidence_interval_95, p_value, is_significant, effect_size, winner.

front: What does CalibrationEvaluator return per case, and where is dataset-level ECE computed?
back: Returns confidence, is_correct, judge_score per case; calibration_ece is aggregated in src/medeval/evaluation/metrics.py.

front: What does ECE stand for?
back: Expected Calibration Error.

front: Interview framing: why is a well-calibrated 70%-accurate model often safer than an overconfident 70%-accurate model?
back: Calibration is about trust, not just accuracy - a well-calibrated model tells you when to double-check its answers.

front: What is medai?
back: A separate, sibling repository - a small clinical-summary service (the 'product') built with a real pluggable LLM client, a real database, and a real test suite that consumes MedEval the way an application team would.

front: Analogy: MedEval is like ___, medai is like ___.
back: MedEval is like pytest or sklearn.metrics - generic, reusable, no idea what your app does. medai is the actual app: the thing that would exist at a real company, with its own DB migrations, on-call rotation, and release cadence.

front: Which direction does the dependency go between medeval and medai?
back: medai depends on medeval (imports it as a scoring dependency). medeval never imports or knows about medai.

front: Does medai listing 'medeval-framework' as a runtime dependency mean the AI depends on the testing platform?
back: No. MedEval's own runtime dependencies are just Python (nothing else) - pytest/black/ruff/pylint are dev-only and never ship. MedEval is a pure scoring library, the same shape as importing sklearn.metrics.f1_score into a production pipeline.

front: What's the difference between offline and online evaluation as used in Section 17?
back: Offline evaluation = pre-deploy CI gates. Online evaluation = continuously scoring live traffic. The same scoring library can serve both purposes.

front: Name real-world LLM-eval tools that follow the same 'runtime dependency, not just dev dependency' pattern as MedEval.
back: DeepEval, RAGAS, Langfuse/LangSmith, and Arize Phoenix.

front: In medai's pipeline.run_case(), what is the call order, and why does it matter?
back: 1) generator.generate(case) - medai calls its OWN AI. 2) runner.evaluate_case(case, prediction) - medai calls medeval to GRADE it. MedEval never calls back into medai.

front: What protocol lets medai swap a fake LLM for a real OpenAI client with zero pipeline code changes?
back: The SummaryGenerator Protocol (runtime_checkable) with a single generate(case) -> Prediction method, implemented by FakeSummaryGenerator and OpenAISummaryGenerator.

front: Where is the 'one translation layer' in medai where ORM records and MedEval dataclasses are allowed to meet?
back: The repository classes (e.g., CaseRepository) in medai/src/medai/repository.py.

front: What do medai's golden_cases.json fixtures demonstrate about testing environments?
back: One pipeline class runs unchanged across three environments: unit tests (fake LLM + sqlite), integration tests (fake LLM + real Postgres), and an opt-in real-LLM smoke tier (real OpenAI + real judge) - zero code changes between them.

front: Interview framing: where does the eval library end and the product begin?
back: The eval library never touches your database, LLM client, or users - it only receives already-produced (case, prediction) pairs and returns metrics. Anything that produces or persists those pairs belongs to the product repo.

front: What are the three implicit phases of every test?
back: Setup (prepare state), call (exercise the thing under test), teardown (clean up, regardless of pass/fail).

front: What is pytest's mechanism for setup/teardown, and where is it usually collected?
back: Fixtures, usually collected in a conftest.py.

front: Why does MedEval's own repository have no conftest.py anywhere?
back: Its tests never touch expensive/stateful external resources (DB, files, network) - every test builds a plain in-memory dataclass and calls a pure function. There's nothing to set up or tear down.

front: What is the general principle for where setup/teardown code should live?
back: Setup/teardown belongs wherever the STATE lives, not wherever the LOGIC lives.

front: In medai's conftest.py, what is db_engine's fixture scope, and what does it do?
back: scope='session' - creates one engine + schema per test session (setup), yields it, then disposes it (teardown).

front: In medai's db_session fixture, what does join_transaction_mode='create_savepoint' accomplish?
back: It lets application code call session.commit() during a test (which only releases a SAVEPOINT), while the real outer transaction is rolled back at teardown - discarding everything, so every test starts from a guaranteed-empty schema.

front: What bug did the meta-test test_database_is_isolated_between_tests actually catch?
back: Golden cases and sample-001 from earlier tests were leaking into a test that never seeded anything - proving the fixture's isolation claim was false until it was fixed.

front: What was the root cause of the test-isolation leak bug in medai?
back: Python's stdlib sqlite3 driver runs its own implicit BEGIN/COMMIT transaction control by default, which conflicts with SQLAlchemy's SAVEPOINT-based nested transactions - so session.commit() committed the REAL transaction instead of just releasing a SAVEPOINT. (Postgres doesn't have this quirk.)

front: What was the fix for the sqlite3 / SQLAlchemy transaction-control conflict in medai?
back: On 'connect', set dbapi_connection.isolation_level = None to disable sqlite3's own transaction control; on 'begin', explicitly emit BEGIN via conn.exec_driver_sql('BEGIN') so SQLAlchemy's SAVEPOINTs behave as documented.

front: How does medai keep its test suite green for contributors without an OpenAI API key?
back: real_llm_client/real_judge fixtures call pytest.skip('OPENAI_API_KEY not set') automatically when no key is configured; only tests marked @pytest.mark.real_llm ever touch the real API.

front: Interview framing: what's the difference between a fixture that 'looks correct' and one that is 'verified correct'?
back: A meta-test that directly asserts the isolation property (rather than assuming the fixture works) - that gap is exactly where the sqlite transaction-control bug was hiding.

front: When is a quality gate 'real'?
back: Only if something actually blocks a bad merge.

front: Why split CI checks into 'required' vs. 'advisory' pipelines?
back: A required check that can fail due to a flaky third-party API or a slow cross-platform matrix trains teams to routinely bypass their own gate. Separate 'must pass before merge' from 'run on a schedule / manually / after specific changes.'

front: List medeval's four Azure Pipelines files and whether each gates merges.
back: azure-pipelines.yml (Yes - full 3 OS x 2 Python matrix); smoke-tests-pipeline.yml (Yes - fast import/wiring checks); formatting-lint-pipeline.yml (Yes - black/ruff/pylint); handbook-examples-pipeline.yml (No - teaching companion only, one job per handbook concept 1-16).

front: List medai's two Azure Pipelines files and whether each gates merges.
back: azure-pipelines.yml (Yes - Unit stage with fake LLM+sqlite, then Integration stage with fake LLM + real Postgres container); real-llm-smoke-pipeline.yml (No - manual-trigger-only, calls the real OpenAI API).

front: How does real-llm-smoke-pipeline.yml ensure it never gates merges?
back: It sets trigger: none and pr: none explicitly.

front: How does real-llm-smoke-pipeline.yml keep the OpenAI API key safe?
back: It reads OPENAI_API_KEY from an Azure DevOps variable group rather than a plain pipeline variable, so the secret is never printed in logs or visible in YAML.

front: What stated reasoning justifies never gating merges on the real-LLM smoke pipeline?
back: 'A required check should never be able to fail because OpenAI is slow or briefly down.'

front: How does medai's Integration stage test against a real Postgres database in CI?
back: It uses an Azure Pipelines service container (postgres:16 image) alongside the test job; only the MEDAI_DATABASE_URL variable changes - same tests, same EvaluationPipeline, same fixtures as the Unit stage.

front: Interview framing: what distinguishes a team that 'has CI' from a team that 'trusts its CI'?
back: Naming which checks are required vs. advisory, and justifying the split by cost/flakiness/speed - not just listing pipeline names.

front: What are the three code-quality tools used, and what is each one's distinct job?
back: black = formatter (canonical style, no debate). ruff = fast linter (unused imports/vars, import order, a subset of flake8-bugbear). pylint = deeper static analysis (design smells, missing super().__init__(), broad excepts).

front: What gate style does 'black --check' use?
back: Fails only on files that disagree with black's own formatting output.

front: What gate style does ruff use?
back: Zero findings required.

front: What gate style does pylint use, and what's the threshold in this project?
back: Score-gated, not zero-findings: --fail-under=9.5 (pylint is intentionally noisier than ruff, so a raw score threshold is used instead).

front: What real bug did pylint find involving Evaluator.__init__ and self.name?
back: Three subclasses (FormatValidator, LLMJudgeEvaluator, CalibrationEvaluator) overrode __init__ without calling super().__init__(), so self.name was never set at all.

front: Why was the missing self.name bug worse than it sounds?
back: EvaluationRunner.evaluate_case() builds its error message using evaluator.name whenever an evaluator raises an exception - so the exception-handling code itself crashed with AttributeError, masking whatever the original error actually was.

front: What was the fourth, unrelated dead-code bug pylint helped surface?
back: base.py's list_available_evaluators() referenced a class called 'FormatValidatorEvaluator', which has never existed - the real class is FormatValidator.

front: What two pylint findings were deliberately silenced (not fixed), and why?
back: logging-fstring-interpolation (the codebase intentionally uses f-strings inside logger calls - lazy %-formatting only saves work when the log level is disabled) and cyclic-import (a deferred, intentional import inside a function body to avoid a real circular import - a false positive).

front: How is the pylint gate different for library code vs. test code in this project?
back: Library code uses --fail-under=9.5 (strict). Test code uses --disable=all --enable=E,W (errors/warnings only), since stricter design/refactor checks that make sense for library code are usually just noise in test code.

front: Interview framing: what's significant about pylint's 9.5 score threshold as a fact to mention?
back: It's a deliberate design choice for library code, not a tool default - and running pylint for the first time surfaced real, previously-unnoticed bugs, proving lint gates catch more than whitespace.

front: What are the 5 steps of the 'practical MedEval mental model'?
back: 1) Model the case with ClinicalCase. 2) Capture the output with Prediction. 3) Choose evaluators for the failure modes you care about. 4) Run them with EvaluationRunner. 5) Use baselines, human review, statistics, and calibration to make release decisions.

front: What are the 5 steps showing how medai and medeval fit together end-to-end?
back: 1) medai's generator produces a Prediction from a ClinicalCase (real or fake AI). 2) medai persists both via its repository layer in an isolated-per-test database. 3) medai hands the (case, prediction) pair to MedEval's EvaluationRunner, unchanged. 4) medai persists the graded CaseResult for later history queries. 5) CI enforces all of this on every PR, with lint/format gates keeping the code itself trustworthy.
